clinicalPearls: An ectodermal dysplasia characterised by reticulate (net-like) hyperpigmentation that, unusually, is not preceded by an inflammatory or vesicular stage
Absent or markedly reduced dermatoglyphics (loss of fingerprints) is a distinctive and helpful sign
Diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and reduced sweating (hypohidrosis) with consequent heat intolerance are typical
Dental anomalies, including yellow-brown discolouration and early tooth loss, and nail dystrophy are common
Autosomal dominant; caused by mutations in KRT14 encoding keratin 14
The reticulate pigmentation tends to fade with age, in contrast to some other pigmentary genodermatoses
Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics, heat-avoidance measures for hypohidrosis, and dental care
reference.pathophysiology: Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome is an autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia caused by mutations in KRT14, which encodes keratin 14, a basal keratinocyte intermediate-filament protein that pairs with keratin 5 to maintain the mechanical integrity of the basal epidermis. The disease-causing mutations affect the non-helical head domain of keratin 14 and are thought to disturb keratin-network function and increase basal keratinocyte apoptosis, with resultant transfer of melanin/pigment into the dermis producing the reticulate hyperpigmentation. The same defect disturbs the development of epidermal appendages, giving hypohidrosis (from reduced or abnormal sweat glands), palmoplantar keratoderma, nail dystrophy, dental abnormalities and the absence of dermatoglyphics. (Mutations in KRT14 that abolish the protein instead cause the allelic dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis.)
additionalDifferentials: Incontinentia pigmenti (which has preceding inflammatory/vesicular stages)
Franceschetti-Jadassohn variants / other reticulate pigmentary disorders
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing pigment incontinence without significant inflammation
Assessment of sweating and heat tolerance
redFlags: Hyperthermia or heat intolerance from hypohidrosis, particularly in infancy
Severe early dental disease requiring intervention
Features suggesting an alternative diagnosis with systemic risk (e.g. dyskeratosis congenita)
reference.prognosis: The condition is compatible with a normal lifespan and general health; the reticulate pigmentation characteristically fades with age. The main ongoing issues are heat intolerance from hypohidrosis, keratoderma and dental problems, all of which are manageable with supportive measures.
pitfalls: Confusing it with incontinentia pigmenti, which has vesicular and verrucous stages preceding pigmentation
Overlooking the diagnostically useful absence of fingerprints
Failing to warn about heat intolerance and to advise cooling measures
Not distinguishing it from the allelic dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis
